Kinetic sampling

Kinetic Langevin Monte Carlo

The exponential integrator, transformed-energy contraction, and the Dalalyan–Riou-Durand manuscript.

Published source; corrected checked proofs

The comparison uses the supplied mainDR_dec_18.tex manuscript. The results prove Wasserstein convergence of the kinetic diffusion, invariance of its Gibbs measure, KLMC and KLMC2 error estimates for correlated Gaussian increments, their Cholesky representations, and explicit iteration counts for a prescribed error. The corrected proofs are unpublished. The reference table records the correction to the continuous prefactor and the stochastic Hessian-difference terms retained in the second-order comparison. The KLMC2 estimate retains the exact fourth Gaussian moment in every dimension; the coarser displayed simplification assumes p≥2. The stronger inverse-step-square exponential term is also proved. Continuous solutions are continuous in L² on finite time intervals. Almost-sure continuity of sample paths is not proved here.

  • Arnak S. Dalalyan and Lionel Riou-Durand (2020). On sampling from a log-concave density using kinetic Langevin diffusions. Bernoulli 26(3), 1956–1988. arXiv

The Brownian kinetic mixing theorem, first-order KLMC sampler theorem, Hessian-corrected KLMC2 theorem, Gibbs stationarity, exact Gaussian and Cholesky constructions, and explicit accuracy corollaries are checked. The source audit records the supplied manuscript corrections and the continuous-L² Brownian model.

Theorems

Kinetic position laws: the complete shifted contraction estimate

Mathematical statement

Let EEE be a complete real inner product space with its Borel structure and a countable topological base. Suppose f:E→Rf:E\to\mathbb Rf:E→R is differentiable and mmm-strongly convex with MMM-Lipschitz gradient, m≤Mm\le Mm≤M. Fix γ≥0\gamma\ge0γ≥0, a<γ/2a<\gamma/2a<γ/2, and 0≤t≤T0\le t\le T0≤t≤T. Let μ,ν\mu,\nuμ,ν be probability laws of the initial position with W2(μ,ν)<∞W_2(\mu,\nu)<\inftyW2​(μ,ν)<∞. Let QQQ be any probability law of the initial velocity and continuous velocity forcing on [0,T][0,T][0,T], independent of the initial position in each process.

The selected flow solves the integral equation, with normalized forcing bt−b0b_t-b_0bt​−b0​,

Yt−Y0=−∫0t(γVs+∇f(Xs),−Vs)ds+(bt−b0,0).Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t(\gamma V_s+\nabla f(X_s),-V_s)ds+(b_t-b_0,0).Yt​−Y0​=−∫0t​(γVs​+∇f(Xs​),−Vs​)ds+(bt​−b0​,0).

Denote its position law by PtQμP_t^Q\muPtQ​μ. Then

W2(PtQμ,PtQν)≤AaekatW2(μ,ν),\boxed{W_2(P_t^Q\mu,P_t^Q\nu)\le A_a e^{k_at}W_2(\mu,\nu),}W2​(PtQ​μ,PtQ​ν)≤Aa​eka​tW2​(μ,ν),​ Aa=2((γ−a)2+a2)γ−2a,A_a=\frac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a},Aa​=γ−2a2((γ−a)2+a2)​​, ka=max⁡{a2−m,M−(γ−a)2}γ−2a.k_a=\frac{\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}.ka​=γ−2amax{a2−m,M−(γ−a)2}​.

This is the explicit prefactor and exponent of the manuscript's equation (exp2), proved for the independent-product laws and the infimum over initial couplings. No continuous Hessian assumption is needed. Choosing a=0a=0a=0 and γ2≥m+M\gamma^2\ge m+Mγ2≥m+M gives 2e−mt/γW2(μ,ν)\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}W_2(\mu,\nu)2​e−mt/γW2​(μ,ν).

The proof first cancels the common forcing in two integral solutions. The earlier strong-smooth gradient interpolation theorem (see ULA-SC, Section 3.10.2) controls the transformed energy ∥V−V′+(γ−a)(X−X′)∥2+∥−(V−V′)−a(X−X′)∥2\|V-V'+(\gamma-a)(X-X')\|^2+\|-(V-V')-a(X-X')\|^2∥V−V′+(γ−a)(X−X′)∥2+∥−(V−V′)−a(X−X′)∥2. Gronwall gives the path estimate. Each initial coupling is then extended by an independent copy of QQQ; both output marginals and its cost are proved before applying the earlier all-couplings transport infimum theorem (see ULA-SC, Section 3.18.4). The specified Brownian source and its Gibbs-stationary solution are also constructed in the supporting modules; the separate KLMC theorem below combines them with the numerical analysis.

The source law may include any common square-integrable velocity and admissible continuous forcing, provided it is independent of each initial position. The noise distribution does not enter the difference estimate because the same realization drives both trajectories. The result therefore separates deterministic contraction from the later specialization to Brownian dynamics.

Convergence of the Brownian kinetic position law to Gibbs equilibrium

Mathematical statement

The Brownian forcing is defined on the stated independent product probability space. The phase path is continuous in L2L^2L2 and is obtained by applying the earlier additive-input existence and uniqueness theorems to the Lipschitz kinetic drift (see ULA-SC, Section 3.14.3, ULA-SC, Section 3.43.2). With standard Gaussian initial velocity independent of the initial position, the selected continuous L² solution solves the kinetic integral equation. Its Gibbs stationarity is proved by an exact Hamiltonian–thermostat splitting limit.

For any finite-second-moment initial law ν\nuν, any a<γ/2a<\gamma/2a<γ/2, and t≥0t\ge0t≥0, its position law νt\nu_tνt​ satisfies

W2(νt,π)≤2((γ−a)2+a2)γ−2a ekatW2(ν,π),W_2(\nu_t,\pi)\le \frac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\,e^{k_at}W_2(\nu,\pi),W2​(νt​,π)≤γ−2a2((γ−a)2+a2)​​eka​tW2​(ν,π), ka=max⁡{a2−m,M−(γ−a)2}γ−2a.k_a=\frac{\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}.ka​=γ−2amax{a2−m,M−(γ−a)2}​.

The theorem takes no stationarity or reference-process premise. The proof constructs the noise, shows that every coupling produces the same output marginals, proves the energy inequality in L², and takes the infimum over all initial couplings. At a=0a=0a=0 and γ2≥m+M\gamma^2\ge m+Mγ2≥m+M, the prefactor becomes 2\sqrt22​ and the exponent is −mt/γ-mt/\gamma−mt/γ.

The stationary comparator has Gaussian velocity independent of its Gibbs position. The kinetic solution preserves their full product law, so its position marginal stays equal to π\piπ. Coupling the arbitrary initial position to that stationary position and using common velocity and forcing yields convergence to equilibrium after the transport infimum is taken.

The first-order KLMC error bound

Mathematical statement

Let f:Rp→Rf:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb Rf:Rp→R be differentiable, mmm-strongly convex and have MMM-Lipschitz gradient, where 0<m≤M0<m\le M0<m≤M. Write π(dx)∝e−f(x)dx\pi(dx)\propto e^{-f(x)}dxπ(dx)∝e−f(x)dx. Choose γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 and h>0h>0h>0 with

γ2≥m+M,4γMh≤m.\gamma^2\ge m+M,\qquad 4\gamma Mh\le m.γ2≥m+M,4γMh≤m.

Initialize velocity as a standard Gaussian independent of the initial position law ν0\nu_0ν0​, with W2(ν0,π)<∞W_2(\nu_0,\pi)<\inftyW2​(ν0​,π)<∞. At every step use the constructed centered Gaussian velocity–position innovation pair with covariance given by the shared exponential Gram kernels; pairs are independent across time and spatial coordinates. Let νn\nu_nνn​ be the position law of this KLMC recursion. Then

W2(νn,π)≤2(1−3mh4γ)nW2(ν0,π)+Mh2pm.\boxed{W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le \sqrt2\left(1-\frac{3mh}{4\gamma}\right)^nW_2(\nu_0,\pi) +\frac{Mh\sqrt{2p}}m.}W2​(νn​,π)≤2​(1−4γ3mh​)nW2​(ν0​,π)+mMh2p​​.​

The first term contracts the initial error; the second is the persistent error caused by freezing the force over a step. The proof constructs the exact and numerical processes together on every initial coupling extended by an independent Gaussian velocity and specified Brownian source. Their common forcing cancels in the contraction estimate. The local freezing error is quadratic in hhh, while geometric accumulation divides by a quantity of order hhh, producing the linear bias above.

The stationary reference is derived from the kinetic equation by a Verlet–OU splitting limit. Exact chain-law identities show that changing the initial coupling does not change the numerical output law. The earlier all-couplings transport theorem (see ULA-SC, Section 3.18.4) gives the initial W2W_2W2​ term; an optimal coupling is not assumed. The construction therefore supplies the reference process and input laws used by the estimate.

The transient is reduced geometrically by increasing the iteration count, whereas the bias persists at a fixed step. A requested accuracy therefore requires choosing the step before choosing the count. The equilibrium velocity second moment is ppp, which explains the dimension factor p\sqrt pp​ in the discretization term.

The KLMC2 bound with the exact Gaussian fourth moment

Mathematical statement

Assume the same strongly convex, smooth potential, and let its Hessian be M2M_2M2​-Lipschitz in operator norm, with M2>0M_2>0M2​>0. Let the initial position have law ν0\nu_0ν0​ with W2(ν0,π)<∞W_2(\nu_0,\pi)<\inftyW2​(ν0​,π)<∞. KLMC2 uses the four correlated Brownian response kernels ψ0,ψ1,φ2,φ3\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3ψ0​,ψ1​,φ2​,φ3​, with the Hessian applied to both the deterministic velocity and the corresponding noise corrections. Initialize velocity with the standard Gaussian law N(0,Ip)\mathcal N(0,I_p)N(0,Ip​), independently of the initial position and the fresh innovations. Suppose

γ>0,γ2≥m+M,0<h,5γMh≤m,45pM2h≤m.\gamma>0,\qquad\gamma^2\ge m+M,\qquad0<h,\qquad5\gamma Mh\le m,\qquad4\sqrt{5p}M_2h\le m.γ>0,γ2≥m+M,0<h,5γMh≤m,45p​M2​h≤m.

Define q=1−mh/(4γ)q=1-mh/(4\gamma)q=1−mh/(4γ), α=(m/(4M2h))2\alpha=(m/(4M_2h))^2α=(m/(4M2​h))2, and

Cp=M2p2+2p+MMp.C_p=M_2\sqrt{p^2+2p}+M\sqrt{Mp}.Cp​=M2​p2+2p​+MMp​.

The Gaussian-chain position law satisfies, in every finite dimension,

W2(νn,π)≤2qnW2(ν0,π)+2h2Cpm+8(M−m)mhe−(α−p)/8.\boxed{\begin{aligned}W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le{}&\sqrt2q^nW_2(\nu_0,\pi)+\frac{\sqrt2h^2C_p}{m}\\&+\frac{8(M-m)}m h e^{-(\alpha-p)/8}.\end{aligned}}W2​(νn​,π)≤​2​qnW2​(ν0​,π)+m2​h2Cp​​+m8(M−m)​he−(α−p)/8.​​

The tail is bounded by both e−p/2e^{-p/2}e−p/2 and e−m2/(160M22h2)e^{-m^2/(160M_2^2h^2)}e−m2/(160M22​h2). For p≥2p\ge2p≥2, simplifying the exact fourth moment yields the supplied manuscript’s displayed bound:

W2(νn,π)≤2qnW2(ν0,π)+2M2ph2m+Mh22Mpm+8Mmhe−p/2.\begin{aligned}W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le{}&\sqrt2q^nW_2(\nu_0,\pi)+\frac{2M_2ph^2}{m}\\&+\frac{Mh^2\sqrt{2Mp}}m+\frac{8M}m h e^{-p/2}.\end{aligned}W2​(νn​,π)≤​2​qnW2​(ν0​,π)+m2M2​ph2​+mMh22Mp​​+m8M​he−p/2.​

The dimension restriction belongs to this final simplification: p2+2p≤2p2p^2+2p\le2p^2p2+2p≤2p2 requires p≥2p\ge2p≥2. The preceding exact-moment bound provides the valid dimension-one conclusion. The source audit preserves the supplied statement and identifies this correction explicitly.

The proof combines a cubic local Taylor–memory error with a contractive comparison of two Hessian-corrected updates. Its force-memory coefficient uses the earlier stationary score moment Eπ∥∇f∥2≤Mp\mathbb E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2\le MpEπ​∥∇f∥2≤Mp (see ULA-SC, Section 3.27.8). The supplied subtraction omits stochastic Hessian-difference terms. The proof retains them and combines the initial Gaussian velocity with the fresh Brownian interval into one stationary free Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Its Gaussian cutoff estimate does not assume independence from the random Hessian. The choice of α\alphaα absorbs the Hessian contribution into the contraction gap. Exact constructed chain and reference laws then permit the Wasserstein infimum. No local-error, stationarity, independence, or convergence conclusion is left as a theorem premise.

An explicit accuracy corollary bounds the entire persistent error term by Bph2B_ph^2Bp​h2, chooses a positive step below both stated stability limits and Bph2≤0.94εB_ph^2\le0.94\varepsilonBp​h2≤0.94ε, and rounds the logarithmic transient count to a natural number. It gives an error at most ε\varepsilonε for the sampler.

The exact moment coefficient is important in low dimension: in dimension one the fourth Gaussian norm moment is three, not a dimension-only square bound of two. The full theorem retains that value. The exponential term comes from the Gaussian cutoff for a possibly dependent random Hessian and cannot be removed from an accuracy claim without a further bound.

The supplied simplified KLMC2 bound, with its valid dimension range

Mathematical statement

Under the assumptions of the exact-moment KLMC2 theorem, suppose additionally that p≥2p\ge2p≥2. Set q=1−mh/(4γ)q=1-mh/(4\gamma)q=1−mh/(4γ). The position law of the same correlated-Gaussian sampler satisfies

W2(νn,π)≤2qnW2(ν0,π)+2M2ph2m+Mh22Mpm+8Mmhe−p/2.W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le\sqrt2q^nW_2(\nu_0,\pi)+\frac{2M_2ph^2}{m}+\frac{Mh^2\sqrt{2Mp}}m+\frac{8M}{m}he^{-p/2}.W2​(νn​,π)≤2​qnW2​(ν0​,π)+m2M2​ph2​+mMh22Mp​​+m8M​he−p/2.

Indeed, p≥2p\ge2p≥2 gives p2+2p≤2p2p^2+2p\le2p^2p2+2p≤2p2, so the exact fourth-moment contribution is bounded by 2M2ph2/m2M_2ph^2/m2M2​ph2/m. The score-moment term is already Mh22Mp/mMh^2\sqrt{2Mp}/mMh22Mp​/m. The cutoff restriction gives α≥5p\alpha\ge5pα≥5p, and hence e−(α−p)/8≤e−p/2e^{-(\alpha-p)/8}\le e^{-p/2}e−(α−p)/8≤e−p/2; also M−m≤MM-m\le MM−m≤M. Applying these nonnegative comparisons term by term proves the displayed bound.

The same cutoff also gives (α−p)/8≥α/10=m2/(160M22h2)(\alpha-p)/8\ge\alpha/10=m^2/(160M_2^2h^2)(α−p)/8≥α/10=m2/(160M22​h2). Thus the final exponential may instead be bounded by exp⁡[−m2/(160M22h2)]\exp[-m^2/(160M_2^2h^2)]exp[−m2/(160M22​h2)], retaining its much faster decrease as the step shrinks.

The dimension restriction is used only in the algebraic simplification of the exact Gaussian fourth-moment contribution. It is not needed to construct the algorithm or its reference. In dimension one, the exact-moment bound remains the appropriate theorem. For smaller steps, the exponential estimate in the reciprocal squared step is sharper than the displayed dimension-only tail.

A uniform condition-number bound for the integer iteration count

Mathematical statement

The source refinement explicitly omits its exponential tail. For m>0m>0m>0, M≥mM\ge mM≥m, M2>0M_2>0M2​>0, p≥1p\ge1p≥1, and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, set γ=m+M\gamma=\sqrt{m+M}γ=m+M​. Let h0h_0h0​ be the minimum of the two source stability limits and εm/(4M2p+2M2Mp)\sqrt{\varepsilon\sqrt m/(4M_2p+2M\sqrt{2Mp})}εm​/(4M2​p+2M2Mp​)​. Put κ=M/m\kappa=M/mκ=M/m, ρ=(M22/3+Mp−1/3)/m\rho=(M_2^{2/3}+Mp^{-1/3})/mρ=(M22/3​+Mp−1/3)/m, and R=max⁡{κ,ρ}R=\max\{\kappa,\rho\}R=max{κ,ρ}. Take a positive finite initial distance DDD, and select n=⌈max⁡{0,(4γ/(mh0))log⁡(24Dm/ε)}⌉n=\lceil\max\{0,(4\gamma/(mh_0))\log(24D\sqrt m/\varepsilon)\}\rceiln=⌈max{0,(4γ/(mh0​))log(24Dm​/ε)}⌉. This natural count obeys

n<1+64[pR2+p/εR5/4]max⁡{0,log⁡24Dmε}.n<1+64\left[\sqrt p R^2+\sqrt{p/\varepsilon}R^{5/4}\right]\max\left\{0,\log\frac{24D\sqrt m}{\varepsilon}\right\}.n<1+64[p​R2+p/ε​R5/4]max{0,logε24Dm​​}.

The exact reciprocal-step identity proves the connection to the physical source parameters. The printed form is recovered under the explicit regime M(1−p−1/3)≤M22/3M(1-p^{-1/3})\le M_2^{2/3}M(1−p−1/3)≤M22/3​. An explicit parameter family shows that no uniform constant bounds the selected reciprocal-step cost by the printed expression without that regime or a correction. This is a statement about the source step prescription; the sampler accuracy theorem above retains its full tail.

The maximum RRR controls two different restrictions: the ratio of upper and lower curvature in the stability branch and Hessian variation in the correction branch. A family with κ=t2\kappa=t^2κ=t2, normalized Hessian ratio one, and p=t6p=t^6p=t6 keeps ρ=2\rho=2ρ=2 while the stability cost grows like t4t^4t4. The proposed expression grows only like t3t^3t3, explaining the extra regime or maximum.

The mathematical argument

The argument below gives the estimates in order, including their constants and analytic justification. The adjacent panels identify the corresponding checked Lean statements and explain their role in the proof.

01The kinetic equation and its Gibbs phase measure §

Let the target potential be fff: the target density is proportional to e−fe^{-f}e−f. The kinetic process has a velocity variable and a position variable satisfying

dVt=−(γVt+∇f(Lt))dt+2γ dWt,dLt=Vtdt.dV_t=-(\gamma V_t+\nabla f(L_t))dt+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,dW_t, \qquad dL_t=V_tdt.dVt​=−(γVt​+∇f(Lt​))dt+2γ​dWt​,dLt​=Vt​dt.

The linear friction γVt\gamma V_tγVt​ removes kinetic energy. The noise amplitude gives a standard Gaussian equilibrium velocity. The candidate equilibrium has density

Π(dx,dv)=π(dx) φ(dv)∝e−f(x)−∥v∥2/2dx dv.\Pi(dx,dv)=\pi(dx)\,\varphi(dv) \propto e^{-f(x)-\|v\|^2/2}dx\,dv.Π(dx,dv)=π(dx)φ(dv)∝e−f(x)−∥v∥2/2dxdv.

Position and velocity are independent under this law. Integrating out velocity therefore leaves precisely the desired target. Thus the position marginal of this phase measure is the target sampling distribution.

Strong convexity supplies a quadratic lower bound on fff, so the partition function is finite and the required position moments exist (see ULA-SC, Section 3.26.10, ULA-SC, Section 3.26.15). A proof of stationarity still needs a solution process and a valid invariance argument; checking that a formal generator integrates to zero is one component of that argument.

The kinetic extension is useful because position is the time integral of velocity even though velocity contains Brownian forcing. This extra time integration reduces the local positional discretization defect. At equilibrium, the Gaussian velocity radius is exactly p\sqrt pp​ in second mean, which determines the dimension factor in the first-order error theorem.

The specified Brownian kinetic flow and its full Gaussian-times-Gibbs stationarity are proved. The proof uses exact Hamiltonian invariance and a controlled splitting limit.

02Normalization of inverse mass §

The general paper equation includes inverse mass u>0u>0u>0: dV=−(γV+u∇f(L))dt+2γu dWdV=-(\gamma V+u\nabla f(L))dt+\sqrt{2\gamma u}\,dWdV=−(γV+u∇f(L))dt+2γu​dW. Its equilibrium velocity has covariance uIuIuI. Normalize both the velocity and the time variable:

Vˉt=u−1/2Vt/u,Lˉt=Lt/u,γˉ=γ/u.\bar V_t=u^{-1/2}V_{t/\sqrt u},\qquad \bar L_t=L_{t/\sqrt u},\qquad \bar\gamma=\gamma/\sqrt u.Vˉt​=u−1/2Vt/u​​,Lˉt​=Lt/u​​,γˉ​=γ/u​.

The position equation becomes dLˉt=Vˉtdtd\bar L_t=\bar V_tdtdLˉt​=Vˉt​dt. Brownian scaling turns u1/4Wt/uu^{1/4}W_{t/\sqrt u}u1/4Wt/u​​ into a standard Brownian motion; substitution in the velocity equation gives the same kinetic system with u=1u=1u=1 and friction γˉ\bar\gammaγˉ​. This is Lemma 1 in the supplied manuscript.

The scaling explains why the rest of the paper fixes u=1u=1u=1: it removes a redundant clock parameter. When transferring a theorem back to another mass, the step size, friction, Gaussian velocity law and physical time must all be transformed together.

To check the transformation, write the position increment as an integral before changing variables: Lt/u−L0=∫0t/uVsds=∫0tu−1/2Vr/udrL_{t/\sqrt u}-L_0=\int_0^{t/\sqrt u}V_sds=\int_0^tu^{-1/2}V_{r/\sqrt u}drLt/u​​−L0​=∫0t/u​​Vs​ds=∫0t​u−1/2Vr/u​​dr. The velocity equation transforms similarly. This verifies the normalized equation for integral solutions, including its initial data, rather than only manipulating differential notation.

The complete inverse-mass integral equation, transformed noise coefficient, Brownian finite-dimensional laws, and independent changed-clock coordinates are proved.

03The difference equation under common Brownian forcing §

Consider two kinetic solutions with different initial positions and the same Brownian input. The random forcing cancels in their difference. Put qt=Lt−Lt′q_t=L_t-L'_tqt​=Lt​−Lt′​, rt=Vt−Vt′r_t=V_t-V'_trt​=Vt​−Vt′​. Then

qt′=rt,rt′=−γrt−Htqt,Ht=∫01∇2f(Lt′+s(Lt−Lt′)) ds.q'_t=r_t,\qquad r'_t=-\gamma r_t-H_tq_t,\qquad H_t=\int_0^1\nabla^2f(L'_t+s(L_t-L'_t))\,ds.qt′​=rt​,rt′​=−γrt​−Ht​qt​,Ht​=∫01​∇2f(Lt′​+s(Lt​−Lt′​))ds.

The averaged Hessian is symmetric and obeys mI⪯Ht⪯MImI\preceq H_t\preceq MImI⪯Ht​⪯MI. The problem has become a deterministic differential inequality along each pair of paths. Existence and uniqueness of those common-input paths follow by applying the earlier additive-input solution theorems to the globally Lipschitz kinetic phase drift (see ULA-SC, Section 3.14.3, ULA-SC, Section 3.43.2). No independent-noise variance is added to this comparison.

The usual Euclidean norm of (r,q)(r,q)(r,q) need not decrease monotonically: energy can move between position and velocity. The paper instead chooses a linear transformation whose squared norm satisfies a differential inequality.

The cancellation takes place before expectations are taken. Consequently the same deterministic estimate holds on every sample path where the integral equations hold, and also in the Hilbert space of square-integrable random vectors. Independent forcing would instead introduce an extra random difference and would not produce this contraction comparison.

Common forcing cancels in the integral solutions. The final theorem applies this argument to the constructed Brownian laws and the Wasserstein coupling infimum.

05The friction regimes and their contraction coefficients §

At v=0v=0v=0 the transformed energy is particularly simple: ∥r+γq∥2+∥r∥2\|r+\gamma q\|^2+\|r\|^2∥r+γq∥2+∥r∥2. If γ2≥m+M\gamma^2\ge m+Mγ2≥m+M, then c(0)=−m/γc(0)=-m/\gammac(0)=−m/γ, so

W2(μPtL,μ′PtL)≤2e−mt/γW2(μ,μ′).W_2(\mu P_t^L,\mu'P_t^L) \le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}W_2(\mu,\mu').W2​(μPtL​,μ′PtL​)≤2​e−mt/γW2​(μ,μ′).

Here the two initial phase-space laws share the same independent velocity marginal. The prefactor is 2\sqrt22​; this follows directly by substituting v=0v=0v=0 in the explicit formula. The supplied source's earlier 2/γ\sqrt2/\gamma2​/γ prefactor in its unshifted display does not match that substitution.

Friction that is very large makes the rate m/γm/\gammam/γ small: velocities are damped before they transport position very far. The smallest friction allowed by this simple estimate is m+M\sqrt{m+M}m+M​. The full table in the paper improves the rate in other regimes by optimizing vvv. For sufficiently large friction it recovers

β=γ−γ2−4m2,\beta=\frac{\gamma-\sqrt{\gamma^2-4m}}2,β=2γ−γ2−4m​​,

This is the slow characteristic rate of a quadratic potential with curvature mmm. This explains the sharpness example. Singular prefactors at a repeated characteristic root require separate limiting estimates.

The optimized exponent and the prefactor describe different effects. A more negative exponent improves long-time decay, while a large prefactor can make a finite-time bound less useful. Near the repeated-root boundary the coordinate transformation becomes singular, so rate optimization must retain its domain and cannot simply substitute the boundary into the prefactor.

All three scalar optimality regimes are proved on the admissible nonsingular shift interval. The Brownian theorem retains the complete prefactor and exponent.

06The exponential update with frozen force §

On an interval of length hhh, replace the changing force ∇f(Lt)\nabla f(L_t)∇f(Lt​) by its value at the current position xxx. The remaining velocity equation is linear and can be solved exactly. Define

ψ0(h)=e−γh,ψ1(h)=1−e−γhγ,ψ2(h)=hγ−1−e−γhγ2.\psi_0(h)=e^{-\gamma h},\qquad \psi_1(h)=\frac{1-e^{-\gamma h}}\gamma,\qquad \psi_2(h)=\frac h\gamma-\frac{1-e^{-\gamma h}}{\gamma^2}.ψ0​(h)=e−γh,ψ1​(h)=γ1−e−γh​,ψ2​(h)=γh​−γ21−e−γh​.

With velocity written first, the update is

v+=ψ0(h)v−ψ1(h)∇f(x)+2γ ξ,x+=x+ψ1(h)v−ψ2(h)∇f(x)+2γ ξ′.v^+=\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)\nabla f(x)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi, \quad x^+=x+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)\nabla f(x)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi'.v+=ψ0​(h)v−ψ1​(h)∇f(x)+2γ​ξ,x+=x+ψ1​(h)v−ψ2​(h)∇f(x)+2γ​ξ′.

The exponential terms handle friction at its exact continuous-time rate. The coefficients of the force are its first and second time integrals. For small hhh, ψ1(h)≈h\psi_1(h)\approx hψ1​(h)≈h and ψ2(h)≈h2/2\psi_2(h)\approx h^2/2ψ2​(h)≈h2/2, which are the first-order velocity and second-order position changes under a constant force.

The only approximation here is freezing the nonlinear force. The linear friction and its associated Gaussian forcing have already been integrated. This is the KLMC exponential integrator reused by KIPLMC1.

An integrating factor gives vt=e−γtv−∫0te−γ(t−s)∇f(x)dsv_t=e^{-\gamma t}v-\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\nabla f(x)dsvt​=e−γtv−∫0t​e−γ(t−s)∇f(x)ds before noise is added. Since the force is constant inside this auxiliary problem, the integral equals ψ1(t)∇f(x)\psi_1(t)\nabla f(x)ψ1​(t)∇f(x). Integrating this velocity once gives the ψ2\psi_2ψ2​ position coefficient. The two coefficient formulas therefore arise from the same exact frozen system.

These are the deterministic update definitions reused directly by KIPLMC1.

07The joint law of velocity and position innovations §

The two random increments come from the same Brownian motion:

ξ=∫0hψ0(h−s)dWs,ξ′=∫0hψ1(h−s)dWs.\xi=\int_0^h\psi_0(h-s)dW_s, \qquad \xi'=\int_0^h\psi_1(h-s)dW_s.ξ=∫0h​ψ0​(h−s)dWs​,ξ′=∫0h​ψ1​(h−s)dWs​.

For each spatial coordinate their covariance is the two-by-two Gram matrix

C=∫0h(ψ0(t)2ψ0(t)ψ1(t)ψ0(t)ψ1(t)ψ1(t)2)dt.C=\int_0^h \begin{pmatrix}\psi_0(t)^2&\psi_0(t)\psi_1(t)\\ \psi_0(t)\psi_1(t)&\psi_1(t)^2\end{pmatrix}dt.C=∫0h​(ψ0​(t)2ψ0​(t)ψ1​(t)​ψ0​(t)ψ1​(t)ψ1​(t)2​)dt.

The off-diagonal entry is positive: both responses integrate the same Brownian increment with positive kernels. Replacing these increments with two independent Gaussians changes the algorithm. Different spatial coordinates and different time intervals use independent Gaussian pairs.

For any real a,ba,ba,b,

(a,b)C(a,b)T=∫0h(aψ0(t)+bψ1(t))2dt≥0.(a,b)C(a,b)^T=\int_0^h(a\psi_0(t)+b\psi_1(t))^2dt\ge0.(a,b)C(a,b)T=∫0h​(aψ0​(t)+bψ1​(t))2dt≥0.

This proves positive semidefiniteness. When h>0h>0h>0, the two coefficient functions are linearly independent, which gives strict positivity. One may therefore sample a pair using a Cholesky factor C=HHTC=HH^TC=HHT and two independent standard normals. A complete law proof identifies this construction with the Brownian integrals and establishes independence from the current state.

For an explicit scalar Gaussian construction, write C00=aC_{00}=aC00​=a, C10=bC_{10}=bC10​=b, and C11=dC_{11}=dC11​=d. Positive definiteness gives a>0a>0a>0 and d−b2/a>0d-b^2/a>0d−b2/a>0. With independent standard normals G,HG,HG,H, the pair (aG,(b/a)G+d−b2/a H)(\sqrt aG,(b/\sqrt a)G+\sqrt{d-b^2/a}\,H)(a​G,(b/a​)G+d−b2/a​H) has exactly covariance CCC. Its nonzero cross term retains the positive cross covariance.

The Brownian convolutions have the specified joint Gaussian Gram law, with independent spatial and time blocks. The sampler law is identified through the joint response construction. The paper’s explicit positive-diagonal Cholesky factor maps two independent standard normals to exactly this same innovation law.

08The local velocity and position errors §

Compare one frozen-force step with the exact kinetic process started at the same phase-space state. Their Brownian terms cancel. Gradient Lipschitzness bounds the velocity defect by

∥Δvt∥L2≤M∫0t∥Ls−L0∥L2ds≤Mt22sup⁡0≤r≤h∥Vr∥L2.\|\Delta v_t\|_{L^2} \le M\int_0^t\|L_s-L_0\|_{L^2}ds \le\frac{Mt^2}{2}\sup_{0\le r\le h}\|V_r\|_{L^2}.∥Δvt​∥L2​≤M∫0t​∥Ls​−L0​∥L2​ds≤2Mt2​0≤r≤hsup​∥Vr​∥L2​.

Position is the integral of velocity, so its defect has an additional time factor:

∥Δxh∥L2≤Mh36sup⁡0≤r≤h∥Vr∥L2.\|\Delta x_h\|_{L^2}\le\frac{Mh^3}{6} \sup_{0\le r\le h}\|V_r\|_{L^2}.∥Δxh​∥L2​≤6Mh3​0≤r≤hsup​∥Vr​∥L2​.

At stationarity ∥Vr∥L2=p\|V_r\|_{L^2}=\sqrt p∥Vr​∥L2​=p​. For the auxiliary exact path started from the numerical state, contraction against the stationary exact path controls its velocity norm by p+Ak\sqrt p+A_kp​+Ak​, where AkA_kAk​ is the current error in transformed coordinates. This prevents the initialization error from reappearing in every step as a fixed additive penalty.

Under the paper's step restriction, combining the two coordinate defects gives the transformed local estimate 34Mh2(p+Ak)\tfrac34Mh^2(\sqrt p+A_k)43​Mh2(p​+Ak​). Constructing the auxiliary process, its moments and the synchronous Gaussian law is part of the analytic proof behind this estimate.

The orders follow from the two scalar integrals: ∫0hsds=h2/2\int_0^hsds=h^2/2∫0h​sds=h2/2, whereas ∫0h(h−s)sds=h3/6\int_0^h(h-s)sds=h^3/6∫0h​(h−s)sds=h3/6. Smoothness is used only to turn the position displacement into force variation. The reference velocity moment, rather than a bound on Brownian path derivatives, controls the remaining stochastic quantity.

The local integrals are bounded in L², and the constructed reference supplies the required stationary Gaussian velocity moments.

Let Ak=∥(ΔVk+γΔLk,−ΔVk)∥L2A_k=\| (\Delta V_k+\gamma\Delta L_k,-\Delta V_k)\|_{L^2}Ak​=∥(ΔVk​+γΔLk​,−ΔVk​)∥L2​. Exact kinetic evolution contracts this transformed norm. A triangle inequality with the one-step defect gives

Ak+1≤(e−mh/γ+34Mh2)Ak+34Mh2p.A_{k+1}\le\left(e^{-mh/\gamma}+\frac34Mh^2\right)A_k +\frac34Mh^2\sqrt p.Ak+1​≤(e−mh/γ+43​Mh2)Ak​+43​Mh2p​.

For 0<h≤m/(4γM)0<h\le m/(4\gamma M)0<h≤m/(4γM), the quadratic correction is small enough to retain most of the continuous contraction:

Ak+1≤qAk+b,q=1−3mh4γ,b=34Mh2p.A_{k+1}\le qA_k+b,\qquad q=1-\frac{3mh}{4\gamma},\quad b=\frac34Mh^2\sqrt p.Ak+1​≤qAk​+b,q=1−4γ3mh​,b=43​Mh2p​.

Induction gives the finite geometric sum Ak≤qkA0+b∑j=0k−1qjA_k\le q^kA_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^jAk​≤qkA0​+b∑j=0k−1​qj. Because 0≤q<10\le q<10≤q<1,

Ak≤qkA0+Mhγpm.A_k\le q^kA_0+\frac{Mh\gamma\sqrt p}m.Ak​≤qkA0​+mMhγp​​.

Equal initial velocities give A0=γW2(ν0,π)A_0=\gamma W_2(\nu_0,\pi)A0​=γW2​(ν0​,π) for an optimal initial coupling; approximate couplings and a limiting infimum work as well. The position projection costs 2/γ\sqrt2/\gamma2​/γ, yielding the displayed KLMC theorem. The recurrence itself is elementary. The substantive stochastic claim is that the chain admits the coupling from which it was derived. Equality of the explicit fresh-noise recursion and its iterated transition laws uses the earlier Markov-law identification (see ULA-SC, Section 3.33.12).

The geometric sum is finite for every iteration count: ∑j=0n−1qj=(1−qn)/(1−q)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j=(1-q^n)/(1-q)∑j=0n−1​qj=(1−qn)/(1−q). Bounding it by (1−q)−1(1-q)^{-1}(1−q)−1 separates transient and persistent errors. Because the local forcing is quadratic and the contraction gap is linear in hhh, the persistent position-error term is linear in the step. The initial-error coefficient remains outside this sum.

The sampler theorem constructs the reference, derives the numerical local inequality, identifies both output laws, and takes the initial-coupling infimum internally.

10The Hessian-corrected exponential update §

If the Hessian is M2M_2M2​-Lipschitz in operator norm, a first-order Taylor expansion of the gradient leaves a quadratic position remainder:

∥∇f(y)−∇f(x)−∇2f(x)(y−x)∥≤M22∥y−x∥2.\|\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x)-\nabla^2f(x)(y-x)\| \le\frac{M_2}{2}\|y-x\|^2.∥∇f(y)−∇f(x)−∇2f(x)(y−x)∥≤2M2​​∥y−x∥2.

The paper inserts the leading velocity and Brownian contributions to Ls−L0L_s-L_0Ls​−L0​ into this expansion. Define φj+1(h)=∫0he−γ(h−s)ψj(s)ds\varphi_{j+1}(h)=\int_0^he^{-\gamma(h-s)}\psi_j(s)dsφj+1​(h)=∫0h​e−γ(h−s)ψj​(s)ds. The resulting KLMC2 update subtracts φ2(h)Hv\varphi_2(h)H vφ2​(h)Hv from velocity and φ3(h)Hv\varphi_3(h)H vφ3​(h)Hv from position, where H=∇2f(x)H=\nabla^2f(x)H=∇2f(x). Its random increments are also corrected by multiplying two additional correlated Gaussian blocks by HHH.

The joint covariance is the Gram integral of (ψ0,ψ1,φ2,φ3)(\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)(ψ0​,ψ1​,φ2​,φ3​). This avoids a matrix exponential: the operations involving the Hessian are matrix–vector products. The second algorithm is therefore more elaborate than the frozen-force integrator, but still explicit.

The name KLMC2 here refers to a Hessian method. KIPLMC2 in the particle paper uses the OBABO splitting and first derivatives; its definition and proof are separate.

The frozen Hessian acts on the displacement generated by the free Ornstein–Uhlenbeck velocity. That displacement contains both the initial-velocity response and fresh Brownian responses. Applying the Hessian to both parts is necessary to obtain the stated higher-order approximation; retaining only the deterministic Hessian–velocity correction would define a different algorithm.

The four-kernel Hessian update and its exact Brownian Gaussian innovation law are constructed. The separate completion audit tracks the chain error bound.

11Fourth moments and stochastic Hessian corrections §

The Taylor remainder contains ∥Ls−L0∥2\|L_s-L_0\|^2∥Ls​−L0​∥2. Its L2L^2L2 norm therefore uses fourth moments. Under the stationary kinetic law, each VsV_sVs​ is standard Gaussian and

E∥Vs∥2=p,E∥Vs∥4=p2+2p.\mathbb E\|V_s\|^2=p,\qquad \mathbb E\|V_s\|^4=p^2+2p.E∥Vs​∥2=p,E∥Vs​∥4=p2+2p.

The kinematic equation Ls−L0=∫0sVrdrL_s-L_0=\int_0^sV_rdrLs​−L0​=∫0s​Vr​dr gives ∥Ls−L0∥L4≤s(p2+2p)1/4\|L_s-L_0\|_{L^4}\le s(p^2+2p)^{1/4}∥Ls​−L0​∥L4​≤s(p2+2p)1/4, without independence between velocities at different times. The proof applies closed-convex averaging to the existing L2L^2L2 time integral. The Taylor forcing is consequently bounded by M2s2p2+2p/2M_2s^2\sqrt{p^2+2p}/2M2​s2p2+2p​/2.

Its damped integral gives the cubic velocity defect. A further force-memory term uses the stationary score bound Eπ∥∇f∥2≤Mp\mathbb E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2\le MpEπ​∥∇f∥2≤Mp from the earlier Gibbs score theorem (see ULA-SC, Section 3.27.8). Integrating the velocity error once more gives the quartic position defect. Proposition 2 is thus for the defined four-kernel step:

∥P−1(Vh−V^h,Lh−L^h)∥L2≤h34(M2p2+2p+MMp),γh≤15.\|P^{-1}(V_h-\hat V_h,L_h-\hat L_h)\|_{L^2} \le\frac{h^3}{4}\bigl(M_2\sqrt{p^2+2p}+M\sqrt{Mp}\bigr), \qquad \gamma h\le\tfrac15.∥P−1(Vh​−V^h​,Lh​−L^h​)∥L2​≤4h3​(M2​p2+2p​+MMp​),γh≤51​.

Proposition 3 requires an additional repair: the source's displayed subtraction omits the Hessian difference multiplying the fresh φ2\varphi_2φ2​ and φ3\varphi_3φ3​ noise. The proof keeps both terms. Write DH=H(L0)−H(L~0)D_H=H(L_0)-H(\widetilde L_0)DH​=H(L0​)−H(L0​), and define the free-OU velocity and complete Hessian responses on the same Brownian interval:

Ur=ψ0(r)V0+2γ∫0rψ0(r−s)dBs,U_r=\psi_0(r)V_0+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_0^r\psi_0(r-s)dB_s,Ur​=ψ0​(r)V0​+2γ​∫0r​ψ0​(r−s)dBs​, Cj(t)=φj(t)V0+2γ∫0tφj(t−s)dBs,j=2,3.C_j(t)=\varphi_j(t)V_0+\sqrt{2\gamma} \int_0^t\varphi_j(t-s)dB_s,\qquad j=2,3.Cj​(t)=φj​(t)V0​+2γ​∫0t​φj​(t−s)dBs​,j=2,3.

Kernel identities, proved by Hilbert-space Fubini and the Brownian isonormal map, give

C2(t)=∫0te−γ(t−s)∫0sUrdrds,C2(t)+γC3(t)=∫0t∫0sUrdrds.C_2(t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\int_0^sU_rdrds, \qquad C_2(t)+\gamma C_3(t)=\int_0^t\int_0^sU_rdrds.C2​(t)=∫0t​e−γ(t−s)∫0s​Ur​drds,C2​(t)+γC3​(t)=∫0t​∫0s​Ur​drds.

Each UrU_rUr​ has the standard Gaussian marginal, proved from the stationary reference velocity and its independent future Brownian interval. The random operator DHD_HDH​ can depend on the coupled positions and velocity; the cutoff argument below requires no independence from UrU_rUr​. The complete correction therefore satisfies, for a≥5pa\ge5pa≥5p,

∥P−1(DHC2(h),DHC3(h))∥L2≤h22[M2a ∥L0−L~0∥L2+2(M−m)e−(a−p)/8].\|P^{-1}(D_HC_2(h),D_HC_3(h))\|_{L^2} \le\frac{h^2}{\sqrt2}\left[ M_2\sqrt a\,\|L_0-\widetilde L_0\|_{L^2} +2(M-m)e^{-(a-p)/8}\right].∥P−1(DH​C2​(h),DH​C3​(h))∥L2​≤2​h2​[M2​a​∥L0​−L0​∥L2​+2(M−m)e−(a−p)/8].

This retains the source constants while accounting for every stochastic Hessian term. The frozen-linear part contracts by 1−mh/(2γ)1-mh/(2\gamma)1−mh/(2γ) under γ2≥m+M\gamma^2\ge m+Mγ2≥m+M and 5γMh≤m5\gamma Mh\le m5γMh≤m; adding the complete correction gives the repaired one-step comparison.

The fourth moment enters because a quadratic Taylor remainder is estimated in second mean: ∥∥D∥2∥L2=(E∥D∥4)1/2\|\|D\|^2\|_{L^2}=(\mathbb E\|D\|^4)^{1/2}∥∥D∥2∥L2​=(E∥D∥4)1/2. Expanding the Gaussian fourth norm gives 3p+p(p−1)=p2+2p3p+p(p-1)=p^2+2p3p+p(p−1)=p2+2p. This exact coefficient is kept until any later dimension-dependent simplification is explicitly justified.

12Gaussian truncation and the second-order sampling bound §

A Gaussian reference velocity need not be independent of the accumulated position error. For any standard Gaussian vector and a≥5pa\ge5pa≥5p, the Gaussian exponential moment gives

∥V∥2≤a+(∥V∥2−a)+,E(∥V∥2−a)+≤4e−(a−p)/4.\|V\|^2\le a+(\|V\|^2-a)_+,\qquad \mathbb E(\|V\|^2-a)_+\le4e^{-(a-p)/4}.∥V∥2≤a+(∥V∥2−a)+​,E(∥V∥2−a)+​≤4e−(a−p)/4.

The Hessian difference satisfies both ∥H(x)−H(y)∥≤M−m\|H(x)-H(y)\|\le M-m∥H(x)−H(y)∥≤M−m and ∥H(x)−H(y)∥≤M2∥x−y∥\|H(x)-H(y)\|\le M_2\|x-y\|∥H(x)−H(y)∥≤M2​∥x−y∥. On the bounded-velocity part use the Lipschitz bound; on the tail use the curvature-width bound. Taking the square root of the integrated estimate gives

∥DHV∥L2≤M2a ∥L0−L~0∥L2+2(M−m)e−(a−p)/8.\|D_HV\|_{L^2}\le M_2\sqrt a\,\|L_0-\widetilde L_0\|_{L^2} +2(M-m)e^{-(a-p)/8}.∥DH​V∥L2​≤M2​a​∥L0​−L0​∥L2​+2(M−m)e−(a−p)/8.

Apply this estimate to each free-OU velocity in the complete correction, then combine the repaired comparison with the cubic local defect. Choose

a=(m4M2h)2,h≤m5γM∧m4M25p.a=\left(\frac{m}{4M_2h}\right)^2,\qquad h\le\frac{m}{5\gamma M}\wedge\frac{m}{4M_2\sqrt{5p}}.a=(4M2​hm​)2,h≤5γMm​∧4M2​5p​m​.

Assume m,M2>0m,M_2>0m,M2​>0, γ2≥m+M\gamma^2\ge m+Mγ2≥m+M, and initial phase law N(0,Ip)⊗ν0\mathcal N(0,I_p)\otimes\nu_0N(0,Ip​)⊗ν0​, with finite W2(ν0,π)W_2(\nu_0,\pi)W2​(ν0​,π). The second step restriction ensures a≥5pa\ge5pa≥5p, and the first enforces the frozen-linear stability bound. The position-dependent comparison term is absorbed into q=1−mh/(4γ)q=1-mh/(4\gamma)q=1−mh/(4γ). Iterating on the constructed common Brownian source and taking the infimum over initial couplings proves for the independently initialized, iid four-kernel Gaussian KLMC2 chain

W2(νnKLMC2,π)≤2qnW2(ν0,π)+2h2m(M2p2+2p+MMp)+8(M−m)hme−(a−p)/8.W_2(\nu_n^{\rm KLMC2},\pi)\le \sqrt2q^n W_2(\nu_0,\pi) +\frac{\sqrt2h^2}{m}\left(M_2\sqrt{p^2+2p}+M\sqrt{Mp}\right) +\frac{8(M-m)h}{m}e^{-(a-p)/8}.W2​(νnKLMC2​,π)≤2​qnW2​(ν0​,π)+m2​h2​(M2​p2+2p​+MMp​)+m8(M−m)h​e−(a−p)/8.

The output transport distance is finite; the real-valued expression does not conceal an infinite distance. No stationary-law, local-error, independence, Gaussian-innovation or optimal-coupling premise is supplied to this final sampler theorem.

The cutoff gives both e−(a−p)/8≤e−p/2e^{-(a-p)/8}\le e^{-p/2}e−(a−p)/8≤e−p/2 and the stronger e−(a−p)/8≤e−m2/(160M22h2)e^{-(a-p)/8}\le e^{-m^2/(160M_2^2h^2)}e−(a−p)/8≤e−m2/(160M22​h2). The printed simplification of the first bias term uses p2+2p≤2p2p^2+2p\le2p^2p2+2p≤2p2, which requires p≥2p\ge2p≥2. Under that explicit restriction the bound implies

W2(νnKLMC2,π)≤2qnW2(ν0,π)+2h2M2pm+h2M2Mpm+8Mhme−p/2.W_2(\nu_n^{\rm KLMC2},\pi)\le \sqrt2q^n W_2(\nu_0,\pi) +\frac{2h^2M_2p}{m}+\frac{h^2M\sqrt{2Mp}}m +\frac{8Mh}{m}e^{-p/2}.W2​(νnKLMC2​,π)≤2​qnW2​(ν0​,π)+m2h2M2​p​+mh2M2Mp​​+m8Mh​e−p/2.

For p=1p=1p=1, the exact fourth-moment expression in the preceding sampling theorem remains the valid conclusion. The source's silently used higher-dimensional simplification is not applied.

The cutoff gives two estimates. Its moderate-velocity contribution is proportional to the current displacement and is absorbed into the contraction gap. Its remaining excess is controlled solely by the Gaussian velocity marginal. Thus the argument remains valid when the displacement and velocity share the entire past of the coupled sampler.

The exact-dimensional theorem is proved for the KLMC2 Gaussian Markov chain, with all reference laws, noise laws, local errors, and coupling infima derived from the stated hypotheses. The printed coefficient is provided with its necessary dimension restriction p at least two; the one-dimensional exact-moment bound is retained.

13Step restrictions and iteration counts for prescribed accuracy §

Suppose an error bound has the form qkD+Bhq^kD+BhqkD+Bh. Choose hhh small enough that BhBhBh is bounded by one part of the error tolerance ε\varepsilonε, and choose kkk large enough for the decaying initial term to satisfy the remaining tolerance. The admissible hhh is the minimum of this accuracy choice and the stability restriction.

For the first integrator, the bias scales as hph\sqrt php​, giving hhh of order ε/p\varepsilon/\sqrt pε/p​, and a step count of order p/ε\sqrt p/\varepsilonp​/ε up to logarithmic and curvature factors. For the Hessian method the leading bias scales as h2ph^2ph2p, giving hhh of order ε/p\sqrt{\varepsilon/p}ε/p​, and a step count of order p/ε\sqrt{p/\varepsilon}p/ε​. These are asymptotic consequences of algorithmic estimates, with fixed geometry constants.

The paper's comparisons keep track of condition numbers as well. A kinetic method gains from smooth position paths, but poor conditioning can make its allowed step size small. The resulting iteration bound therefore depends on dimension, error tolerance, and curvature. A precise complexity theorem also specifies integer rounding and the treatment of already-small initialization error.

The source also gives a finer condition-number comparison after explicitly omitting the Gaussian tail. We can audit that calculation using exact finite expressions. For target error ε/m\varepsilon/\sqrt mε/m​, allocate ε/(2m)\varepsilon/(2\sqrt m)ε/(2m​) to the printed quadratic bias and set

h0=min⁡{m5γM,  m45pM2,  εm4M2p+2M2Mp}.h_0=\min\left\{\frac m{5\gamma M},\; \frac m{4\sqrt{5p}M_2},\; \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt m}{4M_2p+2M\sqrt{2Mp}}}\right\}.h0​=min{5γMm​,45p​M2​m​,4M2​p+2M2Mp​εm​​​}.

Every denominator is positive. This step meets both source stability restrictions and the stated quadratic-bias allocation. Its reciprocal is exactly

Q=max⁡{5γMm,  45pM2m,  4M2p+2M2Mpεm}.Q=\max\left\{\frac{5\gamma M}m,\; \frac{4\sqrt{5p}M_2}m,\; \sqrt{\frac{4M_2p+2M\sqrt{2Mp}}{\varepsilon\sqrt m}}\right\}.Q=max⎩⎨⎧​m5γM​,m45p​M2​​,εm​4M2​p+2M2Mp​​​⎭⎬⎫​.

There is no hidden dimension or curvature factor in this identity. For initial distance DDD, the rounded logarithmic iteration prescription satisfies

n≤1+4γmQ max⁡{0,log⁡24Dmε}.n\le1+\frac{4\gamma}{m}Q\, \max\left\{0,\log\frac{24D\sqrt m}{\varepsilon}\right\}.n≤1+m4γ​Qmax{0,logε24Dm​​}.

This calculation concerns the source comparison with the tail omitted. The sampler accuracy theorem retains the tail and chooses its step using the complete quadratic envelope proved earlier.

To understand the refinement, write κ=M/m\kappa=M/mκ=M/m, η=M2/m3/2\eta=M_2/m^{3/2}η=M2​/m3/2, and

ρ=κ2=η2/3+κp−1/3=M22/3+Mp−1/3m.\rho=\kappa_2=\eta^{2/3}+\kappa p^{-1/3} =\frac{M_2^{2/3}+Mp^{-1/3}}m.ρ=κ2​=η2/3+κp−1/3=mM22/3​+Mp−1/3​.

With γ=m+M\gamma=\sqrt{m+M}γ=m+M​, the source tries to simplify the count coefficient to p ρ2+p/ε ρ5/4\sqrt p\,\rho^2+\sqrt{p/\varepsilon}\,\rho^{5/4}p​ρ2+p/ε​ρ5/4. That simplification drops a factor. A valid refinement is

κρ[p ρ2+p/ε ρ5/4]\sqrt{\frac\kappa\rho}\left[ \sqrt p\,\rho^2+\sqrt{p/\varepsilon}\,\rho^{5/4}\right]ρκ​​[p​ρ2+p/ε​ρ5/4]

This comparison holds up to a universal multiplicative constant and the displayed logarithm. A convenient uniform upper bound uses κ^2=max⁡{κ,ρ}\widehat\kappa_2=\max\{\kappa,\rho\}κ2​=max{κ,ρ}:

C≤64[p κ^22+p/ε κ^25/4],\mathcal C\le64\left[\sqrt p\,\widehat\kappa_2^2+ \sqrt{p/\varepsilon}\,\widehat\kappa_2^{5/4}\right],C≤64[p​κ22​+p/ε​κ25/4​],

Here C=(4γ/m)Q\mathcal C=(4\gamma/m)QC=(4γ/m)Q is the exact count coefficient above. The natural count is therefore less than one plus this bound times the visible nonnegative logarithm. If ρ≥κ\rho\ge\kappaρ≥κ, the maximum is simply ρ\rhoρ, so the printed shape follows with the same explicit constant.

The distinction matters because the modified number discounts gradient curvature by p−1/3p^{-1/3}p−1/3, while the stability restriction still contains M/mM/mM/m. Take a natural t≥2t\ge2t≥2, dimension p=t6p=t^6p=t6, and the valid constants m=1m=1m=1, M=t2M=t^2M=t2, M2=1M_2=1M2​=1, ε=1\varepsilon=1ε=1. A diagonal quadratic potential can have smallest curvature one and largest curvature t2t^2t2; its constant Hessian satisfies the stated Hessian-Lipschitz bound. Here κ=t2\kappa=t^2κ=t2, η=1\eta=1η=1, and ρ=2\rho=2ρ=2 exactly. The normalized iteration coefficient is at least 20t420t^420t4, whereas the source expression is at most 8t38t^38t3. No universal constant multiplying that expression can cover all natural ttt. This diagnoses the source's simplification of the sufficient step and iteration bound; it asserts no lower bound on the best possible behavior of the algorithm.

All inverse-step branches must be retained when deriving a uniform work bound. Inverting a minimum of positive admissible steps produces a maximum of the corresponding positive reciprocal costs. The dominant branch may change with curvature, dimension, Hessian regularity, and requested precision. The integer ceiling then adds less than one iteration to the real logarithmic threshold.

Both samplers now have explicit epsilon guarantees, positive minimum steps, and rounded natural logarithmic counts. The second-order prescription uses the exact dimension term and the proved inverse-step-square tail envelope. The source paragraph that omits the Gaussian tail is also audited: its exact step and natural count are proved, the corrected condition-number envelope has constant 64, and a formal natural-dimension counterexample rules out the unrestricted printed bound.

Compile and verify

git clone https://github.com/odakyildiz/LangevinLean.git
cd LangevinLean
lake exe cache get
lake build KineticLangevin
lake env lean KineticLangevin/Check.lean
bash scripts/check-local.sh

Reproduce the formal proof

Install Git and elan, Lean’s toolchain manager, before cloning. The repository pins the Lean and Mathlib versions. The first cache download requires an internet connection.

lake build checks the Lean proofs. The audit file prints the logical axioms used by the results. The local check script also verifies that every displayed source excerpt matches the repository and that the mathematical pages regenerate correctly. Documentation generation requires Python 3 and Node.js.
